1-a.question: How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?
1-a.decision_correctness_justification: Like the expert, the AI refuses to glob the data folders and instead transcribes a session list from the authors' own `load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m` meta scripts, and it reads the v7.3 files with h5py and the motion-energy files with scipy. But it transcribes only the list used by `Scripts/Figure 8/Figure8a_thru_c.m` (7 animals, 12 sessions) whereas the expert takes every session named in any `load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m` present on disk (14 animals, 44 sessions). It therefore exports 3,116 of 13,762 trials (23%), 520 of 1,954 units (27%), and 7 of 14 subjects. The exclusion of JEB13/14/15 is genuinely well-argued: the AI tabulated DR/WC trial counts per file (trajectory step 70) and showed those sessions have 0-51 WC trials (three have exactly zero), so they cannot support the required WC/DR context output. The exclusion of the entire `RandomizedDelay_Ephys_Behavior` folder (JEB11, JEB12, JEB23, JEB24; 19 sessions) is not argued at all: the AI saw that `loadJEB11/12/23/24_ALMVideo.m` exist (step 23) but never opened them, never listed that folder's contents, and never checked whether those sessions have WC blocks. Those 19 sessions are the same head-fixed ALM/go-cue task with only a randomized delay duration, and the expert included them. Discarding ~43% of the available sessions on an unexamined assumption, against an instruction to 'include all relevant data from the source', is defensible on the record the AI built for the fixed-delay folder but should be checked by a human. The AI also loses the expert's scipy.io fallback for v5 files and the two-probe concatenation path; neither matters for the 12 files it chose, but both would be needed to extend the list.
1-a.code_correctness_justification: `SESSION_SPECS` and `DATA_SUBDIR = 'Ephys_Behavior'` implement exactly the 12-session, single-folder rule described, and `build_dataset` iterates them in order. All 12 files are MATLAB v7.3, so the h5py-only reader succeeds; the script runs end to end in ~55 s and produces 12 sessions / 3,116 trials / 520 units, matching the metadata it writes.

1-b.question: How are the data split into subjects (mice)?
1-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same decision as the expert: the animal is the `<anm>` part of the session key, carried from the hard-coded spec rather than read from `obj.meta.anm` (which the AI inspected at steps 53-54 and found unreliable, the same reason the expert gives). `subjects` is the unique set and `subject_idx` indexes into it per session. The only difference is ordering: the AI orders by first appearance, the expert sorts alphabetically. The format imposes no ordering requirement, so this is immaterial. 7 subjects follow from the session subset judged in 1-a, not from a separate decision here.
1-b.code_correctness_justification: The `subject_to_idx` accumulation produces `subjects = ['JEB6','JEB7','EKH1','EKH3','JGR2','JGR3','JEB19']` with `subject_idx` of length 12 indexing into it, and the verifier's summary confirms the per-subject session counts (JEB19: 4, JEB7: 2, JGR2: 2, rest 1) match `SESSION_SPECS`.

1-c.question: How are the data split into sessions?
1-c.decision_correctness_justification: The unit of a session is identical to the expert's - one `data_structure_<anm>_<date>.mat` file, one entry of `neural`/`input`/`output`/`brain_region_idx`, processed independently by `process_session`, with the probe taken from the authors' meta scripts. The concern is the same as 1-a and is inseparable from it: only the 12 `Ephys_Behavior` sessions become sessions, so the randomized-delay task family is silently absent and the dataset is a quarter the expert's size. Unlike the expert's `session_file`, which searches both task folders so fixed- and randomized-delay sessions are treated uniformly, the AI hard-codes one folder. It also has no two-probe path (`clu[probe-1]` picks exactly one probe); harmless for these 12 single-probe sessions but it would silently halve JEB15's population if the list were extended.
1-c.code_correctness_justification: `process_session` is called once per spec and returns per-session lists that `build_dataset` assembles into parallel session-indexed lists; the verifier reports 12 sessions with consistent per-session neuron counts and a `brain_region_idx` of the right length for each. The `isinstance(clu, h5py.Dataset)` guard would raise on an empty probe rather than produce a silent zero-unit session.

1-d.question: How are the data split into trials?
1-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same decision as the expert: `bp.Ntrials` defines the trial count, every per-trial `bp` field is one entry per trial, spikes carry `clu.trial` (1-based, decremented on read), and camera data are one cell per trial in `obj.traj{view}`, so no trial boundaries are reconstructed. The AI verified the layout empirically (steps 50, 51, 59, 60, 82) before writing the code. The one difference is that the expert's `trial_column` truncates each field to `Ntrials` because a few fields are stored longer, while the AI takes the fields at whatever length they come. I checked all 12 selected sessions: `R`, `hit`, `miss`, `early`, `autowater` and `ev.goCue` are all exactly `Ntrials` long in every one, so the missing truncation changes nothing here - it is a latent fragility only if the session list were extended.
1-d.code_correctness_justification: `load_basic_behavior` reads `Ntrials` and the per-trial vectors consistently; `load_neural_session` uses `go_cue.size` as the trial count while `compute_composite_speed` and `load_motion_energy_aligned` use `beh['ntrials']`, and I verified these are equal on all 12 sessions, so the per-trial arrays that are later indexed by the same `trial_idx` are all the same length. The 1-based to 0-based spike-trial conversion is applied once and correctly.

1-e.question: How are trials filtered based on quality controls?
1-e.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert on both filters the expert applies for reasons grounded in the paper: early-lick trials (`bp.early`) and photostimulation trials (`bp.stim.enable`) are dropped, and ignore (`no`) trials are kept as their own class rather than discarded, so all six outputs share one trial set. The `~early & ~stim.enable` conjunction is lifted from the authors' `params.condition` strings. The expert applies a third filter - dropping trials that run past the end of the recording, which affects two of its 44 sessions - that the AI does not implement. I checked every one of the AI's 12 sessions and the highest trial number carrying a spike equals `Ntrials` in all of them, so no trial in the AI's export is an all-zero post-recording trial and the missing filter costs nothing. The AI also adds a sensible guard requiring at least two surviving trials per session (the format requires it) and treats a missing `bp.stim` group as no photostim.
1-e.code_correctness_justification: `valid_trials = ~early & ~stim_enable` is computed once and used consistently: `valid_idx` selects the neural trials, and the same boolean mask is passed as `keep_mask` into all three `discretize_with_visibility` calls, so the neural, input and output trial sets cannot drift apart. The exported per-session counts in `source_session_info` (e.g. JEB6 382 total, 80 dropped, 302 exported) match `early | stim.enable` counted independently from the raw file.

2-a.question: What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?
2-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source variables as the expert: `obj.clu{probe}`'s `trial`, `trialtm` and `quality` cell arrays, plus `bp.ev.goCue` for the alignment. The AI additionally reads `clu.site` (falling back to `clu.channel`), which it then discards because every recording is ALM and `brain_regions = ['ALM']` - the same single-region conclusion the expert reaches. The only structural difference is that the AI reads one probe per session (the one named in the authors' meta scripts) with no concatenation path, which is equivalent to the expert on every session both include.
2-a.code_correctness_justification: The HDF5 reference chasing is right: `mat['obj']['clu'][()][probe-1, 0]` resolves the probe's struct, and `trial_refs[unit_idx]` / `trialtm_refs[unit_idx]` resolve to the per-cluster arrays, which I confirmed against the AI's own raw dumps of the same fields. `brain_region_idx` is a zero vector of length `n_neurons` per session, consistent with the single-entry `brain_regions` list.

2-b.question: How is the `neural` data processed?
2-b.decision_correctness_justification: Both convert spike counts to Hz and smooth with a Gaussian and do nothing else - no normalisation, baselining or z-scoring - so the stored values are firing rates. The AI is more faithful to the source than the expert: it reimplements `utils/mySmooth.m` line by line, including MATLAB's `gausswin(15)` with alpha = 2.5, the zeroing of the kernel's first half to make it **causal**, renormalisation, and the `'reflect'` boundary (prepend the first N samples, trim after). The expert approximates the same kernel as a symmetric 14 ms Gaussian, explicitly noting it is 'two sided here'. The instructions ask for the SAME processing as the reference code, and `params.smooth = 15` with `params.bctype = 'reflect'` is exactly what every figure script sets; a causal kernel is also the safer choice for a decoder, since a symmetric one leaks post-go-cue spiking backwards across the alignment event. The effective kernel width differs (sigma 2.8 samples = 28 ms at the AI's 10 ms bins vs 14 ms at the expert's 5 ms bins), but that follows from the bin-size decision judged in 2-e, not from this one.
2-b.code_correctness_justification: `gausswin(n, alpha=2.5)` reproduces MATLAB's formula (`sigma = (n-1)/(2*alpha)`, index centred on `(n-1)/2`); `kern[:len(kern)//2] = 0` matches `kern(1:floor(numel(kern)/2)) = 0`; `np.convolve(..., mode='same')` matches `conv(..., 'same')`; and prepending `arr[:n]` then slicing `out[trim:]` with `trim = n` reproduces MATLAB's `x_filt = cat(1, x(1:N,:), x)` with `out = out(N+1:end,:)` under 1-based indexing. Rates are `counts / DT` before smoothing, matching `getSeq.m`'s `N./params.dt`, and are stored as float32 Hz.

2-c.question: How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?
2-c.decision_correctness_justification: Two filters, as with the expert, but both are closer to the source. (1) Quality: the AI drops exactly `garbage`, `gabrga`, `noisy`, `real?` - precisely the `all`-quality branch of `findClusters.m`, matching `params.quality = {'all'}` in every figure script. The expert drops those four plus `poor`, an addition it acknowledges is 'in addition' to the reference. Since 'Poor' is the single most common label in several sessions (17 of 33 clusters in JEB6), this is a real difference, and the AI's choice is the one the authors' code makes. Like the expert, the AI strips and lower-cases the label, having first enumerated the labels per session (step 74) and observed both `'Poor'` and `'poor'` casings. (2) Rate: the AI reproduces `removeLowFRClusters.m` exactly - build the seven `params.condition` PSTHs, then `mean(mean(psth,3,'omitnan'),'omitnan') > params.lowFR`, i.e. mean over time and conditions - whereas the expert simplifies this to the mean rate over all kept trials. Both implement the paper's '>1 Hz' rule; the AI's is the authors' precise estimator. The AI validated the outcome (step 75): 520 surviving units against the paper's reported ~522 ALM units, a genuine external check the expert does not perform. Per-session unit counts (27-67, mean 43.3) are comparable to the expert's (15-110, mean 44.4).
2-c.code_correctness_justification: `quality_is_usable` strips, lower-cases and rejects the four labels; unlabelled clusters (stored as an empty numeric, decoding to `''` or `'[0. 0.]'`) are kept, matching `findClusters.m`'s handling of non-char entries. `get_condition_masks` transcribes the seven `params.condition` strings from `Figure8a_thru_c.m` verbatim. `psth_by_cond` is stacked as (units, time, conditions) and `mean(axis=(1,2))` averages over time and conditions, the same reduction as the MATLAB. Because the PSTH is the trial mean of already-smoothed rates and smoothing is linear, this equals the MATLAB's smooth-of-the-mean; trials with no spikes are included in the denominator in both. Empty-mask conditions fall back to zeros rather than NaN, a negligible difference since condition 1 is always non-empty.

2-d.question: How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?
2-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert and to `alignSpikes.m`: `clu.trialtm` is already on the behaviour clock and relative to its own trial's start, `bp.ev.goCue` is on the same clock, so alignment is the single subtraction `trialtm - goCue[trial]` with no offset or interpolation. Spike trial indices are converted from 1-based. The AI additionally verified (steps 76-77) that `bp.ev.goCue` is populated on WC/autowater trials too (2.5 s, same as DR), so the same alignment is valid in both contexts - a check the expert does not report.
2-d.code_correctness_justification: `aligned_times = spike_trialtm - go_cue[spike_trials]` is computed once per cluster on the whole spike vector after `spike_trials -= 1`, so each spike is referred to the go cue of its own trial. The aligned times are then histogrammed into `edges`, which are defined relative to the go cue, and spikes falling outside the window simply do not land in any bin.

2-e.question: What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?
2-e.decision_correctness_justification: The parameters themselves are well justified: `tmin = -3`, `tmax = 2.5`, `dt = 1/100` are copied verbatim from `Scripts/Figure 8/Figure8a_thru_c.m`, the same script the session list came from, and `get_time_axis` reproduces `getSeq.m`'s bin-centre convention. 10 ms uniform bins, 550 per trial, one grid shared by the neural, input and all three video streams, no rebinning - structurally the same decision as the expert, which uses `getDefaultParams.m`'s 5 ms over -2.5 to 2.5 s. Either parameter set is defensible; both appear in the repo. What makes this concerning is an interaction the AI never noticed. The camera's first frame sits at about -2.47 s from the go cue, so the leading ~53 bins of every trial contain no video at all. In the produced pickle `paw_velocity == 2` on 9.99% of bins and `motion_energy == 2` on 9.96% of bins, against 53/550 = 9.6% - i.e. essentially the entire 'not visible' / 'no video' class is this deterministic pre-video block rather than genuine tracking or video failure, and it is perfectly predictable from the decoder's only input (time from go cue). The expert's -2.5 s start avoids this exactly ('after the correction the frames start at -2.475 s from the go cue, just inside the window'). The neural stream is unaffected - I checked, mean rate in the first bins is 3-5 Hz, not zero, so `clu.trialtm` does extend before the nominal trial start. A human should decide whether to trim the window or accept a semantically hollow third class for two of the six outputs.
2-e.code_correctness_justification: `get_edges()` and `get_time_axis()` are consistent (`edges[:-1] + DT/2`), the same grid feeds the spike histogram, the `input` vector and every video interpolation, and the verifier confirms T = 550 for every trial of every session with an input range of -2.995 to 2.495 s and `time_bin_size = 10.0`. The code implements the stated -3.0/2.5/10 ms decision exactly; the concern above is about the decision, not its implementation.

3-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* derived from?
3-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the expert: the input is not derived from any raw variable but is the bin-centre axis of the analysis window, which is itself defined relative to `bp.ev.goCue` by the alignment. `params.advance_movement = 0` is carried through as a no-op, matching the authors' default. The window differs (-3.0 to 2.5 s vs -2.5 to 2.5 s), which is the parameter decision judged in 2-e rather than a separate one here.
3-a.code_correctness_justification: `input_names = ['time_from_go_cue_s']` with `d_input = 1`, and the verifier reports the input range as -2.995 to 2.495 s, which is exactly the centres of the 550 bins from -3.0 to 2.5.

3-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds*?
3-b.decision_correctness_justification: None, in both solutions - the axis is defined by construction and simply cast to float32 and replicated per trial. The AI's choice to emit the continuous time value rather than a binary onset indicator matches the expert and matches the decoder spec, which lists the input as 'continuous, time-varying'.
3-b.code_correctness_justification: `input_template = taxis[None, :]` gives shape (1, 550) and `input_template.copy()` is appended per trial, so trials do not share a mutable buffer. Values are float32 and monotonic.

3-c.question: How is the `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?
3-c.decision_correctness_justification: Same reasoning as the expert: the input is the centre of the very bins the spikes were histogrammed into, so input element k and neural column k are the same 10 ms interval by construction, with no separate alignment step possible or needed. The three video streams are interpolated onto the identical axis, so all four streams share one time base.
3-c.code_correctness_justification: `get_edges()` supplies the histogram bins in `load_neural_session` and `get_time_axis()` returns the centres of the same `np.arange`, so the two cannot drift. All trials in the exported file have neural, input and output second dimensions of 550.

4-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction* derived from?
4-a.decision_correctness_justification: The expert derives lick direction indirectly from the instructed side `bp.R` combined with the `hit`/`miss` flags, on the stated grounds that 'the lick direction itself is not recorded'. That premise is not quite right: `bp.ev.lickL` and `bp.ev.lickR` hold the actual per-trial lick timestamps for each port, and the AI uses those directly together with `bp.ev.goCue`. This is a measurement rather than an inference, and it is strictly more robust: it does not assume the Bpod outcome flags are consistent with the licks on every trial, and it is better defined in the WC/autowater context where water arrives at a random port and the nominal 'instructed side' is not an instruction at all. Crucially the AI did not just assume this - it dumped the lick cells for `Rhit`/`Lhit`/`Rmiss`/`Lmiss`/`no` trials (step 78) and confirmed the first post-go lick is on the instructed port for hits, the opposite port for misses, and absent on `no` trials, i.e. it cross-validated the direct measurement against the expert's inference before adopting it.
4-a.code_correctness_justification: `lickL_refs` / `lickR_refs` are read as per-trial HDF5 reference arrays and resolved per trial by `read_trial_ref_numeric`, with a `if not ref` guard returning an empty array for null references (trials with no licks on a port). The times are on the same trial clock as `go_cue`, as the AI's own dump confirms.

4-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction*?
4-b.decision_correctness_justification: The rule - earliest lick at or after the go cue decides the side, no post-go lick gives the third class - is a direct reading of the behaviour and produces the same three classes in the same order as the expert (left 0, right 1, none 2, matching the spec's 'left, right, none'). It differs from the expert only where the outcome flags and the licks disagree: across the export `none` occurs on 22.3% of trials against 22.5% ignore trials, so the two definitions nearly coincide but the AI's follows what the animal actually did. Held per-trial constant across bins, as the expert does. One residual ambiguity worth noting, though it is not a defect: a trial where the animal licked only before the go cue is labelled `none` rather than by the direction of that lick; since early-lick trials are already filtered out, this affects very few trials.
4-b.code_correctness_justification: `np.full(..., 2)` default with `first_l < first_r` -> 0 and `first_r < first_l` -> 1 (both `np.inf` when neither port has a post-go lick, leaving 2) implements the stated rule, and the strict inequalities mean an exact tie stays `none` rather than silently favouring a side. `output_values[0] = ['left','right','none']` matches the code order. The 1e-9 tolerance on `>= go_cue` is a harmless float guard. `lick_dir` is computed over all trials and indexed by the original `trial_idx`, so it stays aligned after the early/stim filter.

5-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Behavioral context* derived from?
5-a.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert: the single per-trial flag `obj.bp.autowater`, which marks the water-cued block where reward appears at a random port with no auditory cues. The AI grounded this in the methods text (step 6) and in the authors' own `params.condition` strings, which use `autowater` the same way, and it verified the DR/WC split empirically per session (step 70).
5-a.code_correctness_justification: `bp['autowater']` is read as a per-trial boolean of length `Ntrials` and used directly; no other field contributes.

5-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Behavioral context*?
5-b.decision_correctness_justification: A direct relabelling with the same code assignment as the expert and as the spec: autowater -> WC = 0, everything else -> DR = 1, held constant across the trial's bins. No processing beyond the map.
5-b.code_correctness_justification: `np.where(beh['autowater'], 0, 1)` with `output_values[1] = ['WC','DR']` puts WC at index 0 and DR at index 1, matching the codes. The verifier reports the context output taking only values 0 and 1 (31.5% / 68.5%).

6-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?
6-a.decision_correctness_justification: The same `bp.hit` and `bp.miss` flags the expert uses. The AI additionally loads `bp.no`, but only for the `hit|miss|no` condition mask used in the firing-rate criterion; the ignore class itself is assigned as the default, so the outcome derivation rests on the same two flags as the expert's. The AI grounded the choice in `funcs/getOutcome.m` and the authors' condition strings.
6-a.code_correctness_justification: `hit`, `miss` and `no` are read as per-trial booleans of length `Ntrials`. The outcome assignment uses only `hit` and `miss`, which is sound because the three flags are mutually exclusive and exhaustive in this dataset.

6-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Outcome*?
6-b.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert: initialise to ignore = 2, set miss -> incorrect = 0 and hit -> correct = 1, held constant across bins, with ignore trials kept in the dataset as a third class rather than dropped as the paper does. The code assignment follows the spec's '(incorrect, correct, ignore)'.
6-b.code_correctness_justification: `np.full(ntrials, 2)` then `outcome[miss] = 0` then `outcome[hit] = 1`; since hit and miss are disjoint the order of the two assignments is immaterial. `output_values[2] = ['incorrect','correct','ignore']` matches the numeric codes, and the verifier reports the outcome output spanning 0-2.

7-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue velocity* derived from?
7-a.decision_correctness_justification: The same sources as the expert - `obj.traj{view}`'s `ts`, `featNames` and `frameTimes`, plus `bp.ev.goCue` and the `sglx` bitcode fields for the clock correction - and, like the expert, it uses both cameras because the tongue is visible in only a small fraction of frames and the two views disagree about which. Where the expert takes one feature per view (`tongue`, `top_tongue`), the AI takes all seven tongue features listed in the authors' `params.traj_features` (`tongue`, `left_tongue`, `right_tongue` on view 1; `top_tongue`, `topleft_tongue`, `bottom_tongue`, `bottomleft_tongue` on view 2), skipping any absent from a session's `featNames`. That is a reasonable, source-grounded superset. Also like the expert, the AI does not read the likelihood column, relying on the authors having already set x and y to NaN below threshold - the same rule, reached the same way.
7-a.code_correctness_justification: `load_trial_ts` transposes h5py's (features, xyl, frames) back to (frames, xyl, features), which the AI verified against the raw dumps at step 59, and `ts[:, 0, idx]` / `ts[:, 1, idx]` then pick x and y. `feat_map.get(feat_name)` returning `None` skips features a session does not track, so the seven-feature list degrades safely.

7-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue velocity*?
7-b.decision_correctness_justification: The per-feature half is a faithful, well-evidenced port of the authors' `findPosition.m` and `findVelocity.m`: no smoothing for tongue features (the MATLAB explicitly skips it), linear interpolation onto the analysis grid with NaN propagating through untracked stretches, `gradient` of x and y, NaN velocities set to 0 ('set tongue velocity to 0 if not visible' in the source), speed as the magnitude. The AI even probed scipy's `interp1d` against MATLAB's `interp1` NaN semantics (step 85) to get this right. The problem is the combination step, which is the AI's own invention and is not in the paper: the seven per-feature speeds are averaged **raw**, with no per-view rescaling, even though three come from the side camera and four from the bottom camera at different pixel scales. This is exactly the pitfall the expert identifies and avoids - 'the side camera's 90th percentile is roughly twice the bottom camera's, so they cannot be averaged raw' - by dividing each view by its own 90th percentile before averaging (the same device the paper uses for its kinematic overlays, and `getKinematics.m` likewise z-scores every feature before combining). Because the number of visible features varies bin to bin, the composite's scale depends on *which* subset of views happens to be tracking, so bins where only the side view sees the tongue are systematically offset from bins where both do, and that offset then interacts with the median split. It is not wrong enough to call incorrect - the resulting class fractions (4.77/4.77/90.5%) are close to the expert's (6.23/6.23/87.5%) and validation accuracy is actually slightly higher (0.580 vs 0.572) - but the scale mixing is unjustified and a human should check it.
7-b.code_correctness_justification: The code implements what is described. `per_feature_visible` is computed from the interpolated positions *before* any filling, `np.nan_to_num` is applied only inside a `np.where(per_feature_visible, ...)` so invisible samples contribute exactly 0 to the sum and 0 to the count, and `np.divide(..., np.maximum(visible_counts, 1))` then averages over the visible features only, with `composite_visible = visible_counts > 0`. The `is_tongue = 'tongue' in feat_name` test correctly routes all seven features through the no-smoothing, NaN-to-zero branch.

7-c.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* thresholded into categories?
7-c.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert and to the spec: a single per-session 50th percentile taken over the visible bins pooled across all retained trials and all time points, with `>=` -> 1, `<` -> 0, and the trailing class 2 for bins where the tongue was not tracked. Taking the percentile over visible bins only (rather than over an array where invisible bins are NaN) is the same effective rule as the expert's `np.nanpercentile`, and it is what makes the two visible classes come out balanced (4.767% vs 4.767%). The AI also logs the per-session threshold in `source_session_info`, which the expert does not, making the choice auditable.
7-c.code_correctness_justification: `discretize_with_visibility` computes `np.nanpercentile(keep_values[keep_visible], 50)` after applying `keep_mask`, so the threshold is over retained trials only, and assigns `classes[present] = (keep_values[present] >= threshold)` on top of a `np.full(..., absent_code)` base. The near-exact 50/50 split of the two visible classes in the output confirms the threshold is being applied to the same population it was computed from. The `threshold is None` path (no visible bins at all) correctly leaves the whole session as class 2.

7-d.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* aligned with the neural data?
7-d.decision_correctness_justification: The same two-step correction as the expert, from the same source: a session-constant video offset from the bitcode pulse recorded on both clocks (`mode(sglx.bitcode.bitstart)/sglx.fs - mode(bp.ev.bitStart)`, a port of `findVideoOffset.m`), then `frameTimes - vidshift - goCue[trial]`, then onto the shared bin grid so the camera and the spikes have one time axis. The AI verified the offset numerically on a session before building it in (step 84: 0.49004 s). Where the expert averages the frames falling inside each bin, the AI linearly interpolates onto the bin centres, which is what the authors' `findPosition.m` does; at 400 Hz video into 10 ms bins that discards a little information but is the source-faithful choice. Frames outside the window yield NaN and hence the `not visible` class in both solutions.
7-d.code_correctness_justification: `matlab_mode` reproduces MATLAB's `mode` (smallest most-frequent value, NaNs excluded) and the offset is `mode(bitstart)/fs - mode(bitStart)`, algebraically the same as the expert's `mode(bitstart/fs) - mode(bitStart)` since `fs` is a constant. `old_t = frame_times - vidshift - align_time` is passed as the source abscissa to `interp_with_nans`, whose `bounds_error=False, fill_value=np.nan` correctly produces NaN (and hence class 2) outside the frame range.

8-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Paw velocity* derived from?
8-a.decision_correctness_justification: Both use the bottom camera's paw tracking in `obj.traj`. The expert uses `top_paw` alone, on the reasoned grounds that `bottom_paw`'s likelihood oscillates through the delay epoch and the two are different forepaws rather than two views of one. The AI uses both `top_paw` and `bottom_paw` - the full view-2 paw set from the authors' `params.traj_features` - and averages over whichever is visible per bin. This is equally defensible and avoids the expert's concern in practice for two reasons: both features are on the same camera so they share a pixel scale (unlike the tongue case in 7-b), and the per-bin visible-only averaging means `bottom_paw`'s dropout does not inject a spurious value, the composite simply falls back to `top_paw`. It does mean the composite's scale shifts slightly between bins where one versus two paws are tracked, and it conflates two anatomically distinct effectors into one 'paw velocity'. The resulting class fractions (44.8/44.8/10.5%) are close to the expert's (40.7/40.7/18.6%) and validation accuracy is higher (0.570 vs 0.541). The AI gives no explicit reason for using both, which is the main weakness relative to the expert's argued choice.
8-a.code_correctness_justification: `PAW_FEATURES = [(2,'top_paw'), (2,'bottom_paw')]` is passed through the same `compute_composite_speed` machinery, `views_needed` resolves to view 2 only, and the visible-only averaging behaves as described. A session missing `bottom_paw` from `featNames` silently falls back to `top_paw` alone.

8-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Paw velocity*?
8-b.decision_correctness_justification: The AI routes the paw through the **non-tongue** branch of the authors' code and ports it exactly: nearest-fill the interpolated positions (`fillmissing(...,'nearest')` in `findPosition.m`), `gradient`, subtract a baseline derivative `median(diff(x))` from the velocity, nearest-fill the velocities, speed as the magnitude, in pixels per bin. The expert instead smooths x and y with a 5 ms Gaussian within each contiguous run of tracked frames and differentiates against the real frame times, giving pixels per second, and does not subtract a baseline. Both are reasonable; the AI's is more faithful to the source, which the instructions ask for, and since the discretisation is a within-session median split the units are irrelevant. Two things temper this. First, the AI faithfully reproduces what looks like a bug in the authors' `findVelocity.m` - `yvel = yvel - basederiv(1)`, i.e. the *x* baseline is subtracted from the *y* velocity - which is the right call under 'use the SAME processing' but is worth a human being aware of. Second, filling positions before differentiating means the derivative at the edges of a tracking gap is computed against a held-constant value rather than real data; the expert's per-run approach avoids this. In practice those bins are labelled not-visible and never thresholded, so the effect is confined to the one or two bins adjacent to each gap.
8-b.code_correctness_justification: The non-tongue branch matches `findVelocity.m` line for line, including the `basederiv(1)`-to-both-axes quirk, and `fill_nearest_1d` is a correct vectorised `fillmissing(...,'nearest')` (the `(idx - prev_idx) <= (next_idx - idx)` tie-break favours the earlier sample, as MATLAB does). Critically, `visible` is captured from `x_interp`/`y_interp` *before* `fill_nearest_1d` is applied, so filled stretches are labelled not-visible and never enter the percentile or the classes - the fill cannot fabricate a movement class. The all-NaN guard (`if np.any(np.isfinite(xpos))`) prevents the `nanmedian`-of-empty warning the AI hit on its first run.

8-c.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* thresholded into categories?
8-c.decision_correctness_justification: The same rule as the tongue and as the expert: per-session 50th percentile over the visible bins, `>=` -> 1, `<` -> 0, untracked -> 2, with the threshold logged per session. The resulting split is balanced (44.75% / 44.76%). The one substantive caveat is inherited from the window decision judged in 2-e rather than from this rule: about 96% of the class-2 bins are the deterministic -3.0 to -2.47 s pre-video block present on every trial, not genuine tracking failure, so 'not visible' here means something weaker than in the expert's export (18.6% class 2, reflecting real dropout). I have scored that concern once, at 2-e, rather than re-charging it here.
8-c.code_correctness_justification: The same verified `discretize_with_visibility` call, with `absent_code=2` and `output_values[4] = ['<50th_percentile','>=50th_percentile','not_visible']` in matching order. The near-exact 50/50 split of the visible classes confirms correct application.

8-d.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* aligned with the neural data?
8-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert: same session video offset, `frameTimes - vidshift - goCue[trial]`, then onto the shared bin grid. Like the expert, the AI takes the frame times from the camera that actually carries the feature (bundles are fetched per requested view) rather than always from the side camera, which is the detail the expert calls out as necessary because the two cameras can record different numbers of frames in a trial.
8-d.code_correctness_justification: `views_needed` is derived from the feature specs, so the paw pass loads only view 2 and `bundles[view]` supplies that view's own `frame_times` to `old_t`. The same `vidshift` is used for every stream in the session.

9-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Motion energy* derived from?
9-a.decision_correctness_justification: The same choice as the expert: the standalone `motionEnergy_<anm>_<date>.mat` beside the data structure, taking `me.data` as one trace per trial with one value per camera frame, and ignoring `obj.me` (which exists in only some sessions) and `me.moveThresh` (the authors' own movement threshold, superseded by the spec's median split). The AI inspected the file layout directly (steps 67-68) before committing. One gap: it does not port `loadMotionEnergy.m`'s `if isstruct(me.data), me.data = me.data.data; end` guard, which the expert reproduces as an unwrapping loop because three of the 44 files wrap the data twice. None of the AI's 12 files needs it, so nothing is wrong in the delivered export, but the reader would break rather than degrade if the session list were extended.
9-a.code_correctness_justification: `sio.loadmat(..., squeeze_me=True, struct_as_record=False)` then `me.data` reshaped to a 1-D object array of per-trial traces, indexed by `trial_idx`, works on all 12 files (the conversion completes and produces sensible per-session thresholds, e.g. 15.57 for JEB6). The `if not motion_path.exists()` path correctly yields an all-`no_video` output rather than crashing.

9-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Motion energy*?
9-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same conclusion as the expert: motion energy is already one scalar per frame (the spatial reduction is done upstream by the authors), so there is nothing to smooth, differentiate or combine - only align and resample. The AI interpolates onto the bin grid (per `loadMotionEnergy.m`'s `interp1`) where the expert averages frames into bins; both are reasonable resampling choices and the AI's is the source-faithful one. The AI also ports `fillmissing(me.data,'nearest')`, but records visibility before filling so the fill never affects the result - a sensible way to honour both the MATLAB and the spec's requirement for a distinct `no video` class, which the authors' fill would otherwise erase.
9-b.code_correctness_justification: `visible[trial_idx,:] = np.isfinite(trial_aligned)` is set before `aligned[trial_idx,:] = fill_nearest_1d(trial_aligned)`, and `discretize_with_visibility` uses only `keep_values[keep_visible]` for both the percentile and the class assignment, so the filled values are genuinely inert - they are computed and then never read (see 11-d).

9-c.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* thresholded into categories?
9-c.decision_correctness_justification: The same per-session 50th-percentile rule as the tongue, the paw and the expert, with the trailing class relabelled `no_video` per the spec. The split is balanced (45.0% / 45.2%). Choosing the spec's median split over the authors' own `me.moveThresh` is correct - the spec is explicit. As with the paw, the 9.77% `no_video` fraction is dominated by the structural pre-video window rather than by sessions genuinely lacking video (the expert's is 3.8% and reflects real gaps); that is the window decision already charged at 2-e. Note this did not translate into inflated performance - the AI's motion-energy validation accuracy is 0.671 against the expert's 0.719.
9-c.code_correctness_justification: The same verified `discretize_with_visibility` call with `absent_code=2`, and `output_values[5] = ['<50th_percentile','>=50th_percentile','no_video']` in matching order - correctly using the spec's distinct 'no video' wording for this output rather than 'not visible'.

9-d.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* aligned with the neural data?
9-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the expert: motion energy has one value per frame of the side camera, so `obj.traj{1}`'s `frameTimes` are corrected by the session offset and the trial's go cue and then resampled onto the shared grid. This is exactly what `loadMotionEnergy.m` does, and the AI took the view-1 choice from there.
9-d.code_correctness_justification: `load_trial_video_bundle(mat, traj_groups[0], trial_idx)` fetches view 1, `old_t = frame_times - vidshift - beh['goCue'][trial_idx]` applies the same correction as the other streams, and a trial whose view-1 bundle is unavailable is `continue`d, leaving it NaN and therefore `no_video`.

10.question: How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?
10.decision_correctness_justification: The overall philosophy matches the expert's - keep the trial, mark the gap, never drop a trial because its video is bad, since its neural and behavioural data are unaffected - and the AI covers more failure modes than the expert does (missing `clu.site` falling back to `clu.channel`, missing `bp.stim`, missing motion-energy file, features absent from `featNames`, null HDF5 references, all-NaN velocity). Untracked frames are handled the same way in both: the positions are already NaN, visibility is recorded before any filling, and the bin gets the trailing class, so no fabricated value is ever thresholded. The one real divergence is the missing-`frameTimes` case. The expert returns early and marks the trial not-visible. The AI substitutes a synthetic 400 Hz clock `(arange(n)+1)/400`, copied from `findPosition.m`'s fallback - but that MATLAB fallback is for when the *field is absent*, and after subtracting `vidshift` and `goCue` the synthetic times land those frames at roughly -3.0 to -0.5 s regardless of when they were actually recorded, so the trial gets misaligned video rather than an honest gap. I measured the exposure: it fires on 4 of 7,252 trial-view pairs in the export, so the practical impact is negligible, but fabricating an alignment is a weaker choice than the expert's honest gap and is the reason this is OK rather than MATCH.
10.code_correctness_justification: Each guard does what is described: the `NdroppedFrames` NaN check returns `(None, None)` and the caller skips; `interp_with_nans` returns an all-NaN row when fewer than two finite abscissae survive; `fill_nearest_1d` short-circuits on all-valid and all-invalid input; the `site`/`channel`/`None` chain is exhaustive. No NaN reaches the pickle - the reference verifier ran on the output with zero errors and zero warnings.

11-a.question: What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?
11-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI reaches the same broad situation as the expert - file reading dominates and computation is cheap - but for a different and partly self-inflicted reason, and it never diagnosed this. I profiled one session (JEB6, 382 trials, 5.9 s): `load_trial_video_bundle` is 4.0 s (68%), essentially all of it h5py reads of the per-trial `ts` arrays (10,132 dataset reads, 3.2 s); motion-energy alignment adds 1.0 s; the neural histogram-and-smooth loop only 0.85 s. Total conversion is ~55 s for 12 sessions, against the expert's ~135 s for 44 - comparable per session. The difference from the expert is that the expert's loading cost is irreducible ('the data has to be read once either way'), whereas the AI's is not: it reads the same video arrays four times per trial (see 11-c). The AI's only stated view is wrong - at step 94 it attributed the runtime to 'rebuilding smoothed trial-by-trial firing rates and aligned video features' when the profile shows the neural path is 14% of it. Rated OK rather than lower because the outcome is an acceptably fast script and no correctness consequence follows.
11-a.code_correctness_justification: The code does perform the work the profile attributes to it; there is no discrepancy between behaviour and description. The hot path is genuinely `load_trial_ts`'s `np.asarray(mat[ref][()])`, which materialises the full (frames, 3, features) array on every call.

11-b.question: What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?
11-b.decision_correctness_justification: The AI leaves more loops un-vectorised than the expert. The clearest is spike counting: it runs a nested `for unit: for trial: np.histogram(...)` - roughly 11,300 one-dimensional histograms per session, each rescanning the cluster's whole spike vector via `aligned_times[spike_trials == tr]` - where the expert collapses the entire unit into a single `np.histogram2d(spike_trial, spike_time, bins=[trial_edges, BIN_EDGES])`. `my_smooth` also loops over columns when the whole (trials, bins) block could go through one `convolve1d`. The per-trial video loops are the same situation the expert describes and defends - each trial has a different number of frames, so there is no rectangular array - though the seven tongue features of a view could be interpolated in one `interp1d` call with a 2-D `y` instead of fourteen separate ones. Since the spike path is only 14% of runtime and the script finishes in under a minute, none of this matters in practice, which is why this is OK rather than concerning; but the expert made the one vectorisation that counted and the AI did not.
11-b.code_correctness_justification: The loops are correct, just not fast: the per-trial histogram produces the same counts as a 2-D histogram would, and `my_smooth`'s per-column convolution is equivalent to filtering the block. The vectorised parts that do exist (`aligned_times = spike_trialtm - go_cue[spike_trials]`, `fill_nearest_1d`'s accumulate-based nearest fill, the `np.where`/`np.divide` composite) are implemented correctly.

11-c.question: What processing does the code repeat multiple times?
11-c.decision_correctness_justification: This is the clearest regression against the expert, which states plainly that 'nothing is recomputed - each file is read once, the video offset is computed once per session rather than per trial, each feature's frame-resolution velocity is computed once and reused'. The AI structures the three video outputs as three independent passes over the session, so: `load_trial_video_bundle` runs four times per trial (views 1 and 2 for the tongue, view 2 again for the paw, view 1 again for motion energy), each call re-reading the full `ts` array off disk; `get_video_offset` - a session constant - is recomputed three times per session, each time re-reading `sglx.fs`, `sglx.bitcode.bitstart` and `bp.ev.bitStart` and re-running `matlab_mode`; `load_traj_groups` runs three times and `get_feature_maps` twice; `get_time_axis()`/`get_edges()` rebuild the same `np.arange` on every call, thousands of times per session; and `fill_nearest_1d` is applied twice along the paw path (positions, then velocities). This is measurable, not theoretical: redundant bundle loading is roughly a third of total runtime, so caching one bundle per view per trial would cut the conversion by about that much. Nothing about it is incorrect - the recomputed values are identical each time - but it is an avoidable structural inefficiency that a reviewer should fix, and the AI never noticed it.
11-c.code_correctness_justification: The repeated computations are deterministic and produce identical results on each call (`get_video_offset` depends only on session-level fields, `get_time_axis` only on module constants), so the redundancy costs time but cannot introduce inconsistency between streams - indeed it guarantees all three streams use the same offset and the same axis.

11-d.question: What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?
11-d.decision_correctness_justification: The AI has somewhat more dead work than the expert, which claims none beyond the loader materialising unused fields. Concretely: `clu.site`/`clu.channel` is read for every kept unit, filtered by the firing-rate mask, returned from `load_neural_session` and then never referenced - `brain_region_idx` is a hard-coded zero vector because every recording is ALM, so the whole `sites` plumbing is dead (it looks like an anticipated depth annotation the single-region decision made moot). `bp.L`, `bp.ev.sample` and `bp.ev.delay` are loaded and unused; `bp.no` is loaded but redundant since ignore is the default class; `bitStart` is reused to compute a `bit_start_offset_s` metadata field nothing consumes. `fill_nearest_1d` on the aligned motion energy is computed and then never read, since both the percentile and the class assignment use only pre-fill visible bins. Seven condition PSTHs are built to feed a single scalar criterion, two pairs of which differ only by `~early`. And the video streams are computed for all trials including the ~9% dropped as early/stim, which the neural path needs (for the condition masks) but the video path does not. All of it is cheap relative to the I/O, so this is a tidiness issue rather than a performance one.
11-d.code_correctness_justification: The unused computations are genuinely inert - `sites[use]` is returned into a variable that is never read again, and the motion-energy fill writes into `aligned` at positions that `discretize_with_visibility` masks out - so none of them can affect the exported values. The output the verifier checked contains no trace of them.
